To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the processing of hypothetical contexts is associated with a frontal P600-like effect.

(i) a P600-like positivity is sensitive to cross-sentential referent dependencies in auditorily presented sentences, (ii) this positivity is sensitive to the distinction between reference in the real and hypothetical worlds, and (iii) the effect of the latter distinction can be observed in the absence of a real referent.

(i) the P600-like positivity is elicited by the pronoun in the sentence ‘It ends quite abruptly’, when the pronoun is dependent on the novel mentioned in the previous sentence, but not when the pronoun’s antecedent is a hypothetical novel mentioned in the sentence ‘John is considering to write a novel’; (ii) this effect was observed when the sentences were auditorily presented; (iii) the effect was observed in a frontal-central region, and was not observed
In summary, our research is concerned with

the interaction between two types of information: (i) the referential dependencies across utterances in a discourse, and (ii) information about the type of discourse (i.e. actual vs. hypothetical) in which the utterances are embedded.
the interaction of the discourse level with the syntactic level of language comprehension.

the role of context in discourse processing, and the interaction between the two dimensions of context: (i) reference to events/situation versus entities/individuals, and (ii) reference in actual versus hypothetical worlds.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the N400 effect in the context of a hypothetical sentence does not occur, and the P600-like frontal positive effect does occur, in response to the pronoun in a hypothetical sentence, compared to the pronoun embedded in a nonhypothetical sentence.
there is a P600-like positivity for hypothetical contexts in auditorily presented sentences, which is not modulated by referential dependencies.

this study provides evidence for an interaction between the two dimensions of discourse processing: referential dependencies across sentence boundaries and the distinction between reference in real and hypothetical worlds.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ERPs can be used to study discourse-level language processing, including referential dependencies, in the real and hypothetical worlds.

the P600 is a general marker of the integration of new information with the preceding linguistic context, and the frontal positivity is an index of the processing of hypothetical information in discourse.
the brain uses multiple levels of linguistic and non-linguistic information to interpret pronouns.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the P600-like frontal negativity is sensitive to both referential dependencies and hypothetical contexts.
discourse-level language processing is sensitive to the distinction between real and hypothetical contexts, and that this distinction is reflected in the brain’s response to sentences.
the brain is sensitive to both referential dependencies and the distinction between actual and hypothetical worlds.
